answer: Ledgerly uses **Django** as its backend framework with **Django REST Framework**. The team started with a Django monolith architecture rather than microservices.
We store all money as integer cents in bigint columns, never as floats or Decimal in the database. Rounding happens once, when we render the invoice.

Stripe is the payment provider Ledgerly uses for new customers. The decision was made in March 2026 because Stripe supports SEPA Direct Debit and has better-documented webhooks compared to the Mollie alternative.

Stripe charges a percentage on SEPA Direct Debit transactions, whereas Mollie charges a flat fee per transaction, which is much cheaper for invoices above 100 euros. The team switched to Mollie in June 2026 to reduce payment processing costs.

Invoice numbers follow the format `LDG-YYYY-NNNNN` (e.g., `LDG-2026-00042`), with the counter resetting every January. Numbers must be gapless due to German tax rules (GoBD), so they're allocated within the same transaction that finalizes the invoice.

Invoice numbers must have no gaps because German tax rules (GoBD) do not allow holes in the sequence. To comply, the team allocates invoice numbers within the same transaction that finalizes the invoice.

Puppeteer (headless Chrome) was crashing because it required more than the 512 MB of memory available in the team's container. WeasyPrint renders HTML templates without needing a browser engine, making it suitable for their memory-constrained environment.
Tests run against a real Postgres database started with testcontainers. The team switched from SQLite because it hid bugs with bigint and row locking.

The server was running in UTC and derived the invoice date from a UTC timestamp, which caused invoices to be dated one day too early when finalized shortly after midnight (local Berlin time). The fix was to derive `issued_on` from the Europe/Berlin local date instead and add a test for 00:30 local time.

The team chose Postmark over SendGrid because in testing, SendGrid emails landed in spam at GMX and web.de, which most of their German customers use. Postmark had better deliverability for those providers.
Users log in to Ledgerly with magic links sent by email; the links expire after 15 minutes and work once. The team decided not to store passwords at all.
No, Unleash was removed in June 2026 because it was overkill and required constant server updates; the team replaced it with environment variables read at startup.

The team added an idempotency key on the payment intent id with a unique constraint in the database, so retried webhooks become no-ops and don't create duplicate payment records. This prevents the issue where Stripe retries would create a second payment when the first webhook timed out.
The Pro plan costs 29 euros per month. It adds automatic dunning as a feature compared to the Starter plan.
Dunning reminders are sent 7, 14, and 30 days after the due date. The third reminder also adds a late fee.
The public API allows 60 requests per minute per API key, and requests exceeding this limit receive a 429 response with a Retry-After header.
The team keeps database backups for **30 days**, with nightly pg_dump backups to S3-compatible object storage at Hetzner and monthly restore tests on the first Monday of each month.
The team uses **i18next** for translations. They wrap every string with i18next instead of hardcoding German text, since the UI is German first with English to come later.
